name: NIS 2 Directive
evidence_rating: thin: forecasts only; outcome data limited to ENISA's descriptive surveys; no causal study of NIS1 or NIS2 effects on incidents or costs
summary: The Commission expected NIS 2 to cut the cost of cyber incidents by EUR 11.3 billion over ten years, at the price of up to 22% more security spending for newly covered firms. Neither figure has been measured: ENISA's surveys show security budgets steady at about 9% of IT spending, compliance as the main driver of investment, and newly covered sectors lagging behind those already regulated. Transposition was slow - four countries were taken to court in July 2026 - and no study yet measures whether incidents have fallen.

indicators.objective: The NIS 2 proposal's financial statement lists no result indicators (its 1.4.4 covers synergies); monitoring indicators are set out in Annexes 11-12 of the impact assessment and rely on ENISA's investment survey and State of Cybersecurity report
Raise cyber resilience across all relevant sectors
indicators.indicator: Sector-specific ICT security spending as % of ICT spending converging (target: within 1 pp of sector average)
indicators.target_or_baseline: IA baseline: no data on NIS1's effect on security spending
indicators.evidence: ENISA's annual survey tracks the share of IT budgets spent on information security: 7.1% (2023 report), 9.0% (2024, n=1,350), about 9% again in 2025 (median EUR 1.5m). 2024 data are a pre-NIS2 baseline; sector convergence not yet assessed against the target.

indicators.indicator: ICT security spending increase of up to 22% in first years for newly covered entities (12% for entities already under NIS1)
indicators.evidence: Not measured directly. ENISA 2024: most organisations expect a one-off or permanent budget increase for NIS2; 89% say they need more security staff; 34% of SMEs say they cannot ask for the extra budget. ENISA 2025: compliance is the main driver of security investment for 70% of organisations.

indicators.indicator: Reduction in cost of cybersecurity incidents of EUR 11.3bn over ten years
indicators.evidence: Not measured. No EU-level series on incident costs exists; the IA itself notes the lack of systematic data. ENISA 2025 reports 28% of organisations take over three months to patch critical vulnerabilities and 30% did no security assessment in the past year.

indicators.indicator: Resources of competent authorities up about 20-30%
indicators.evidence: No systematic data found on authorities' resources since 2023.

indicators.indicator: Timely and consistent transposition; peer reviews and comparative assessments
indicators.evidence: Transposition slow: letters of formal notice (28 Nov 2024) and reasoned opinions (7 May 2025) to the laggards; in July 2026 Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands were referred to the Court of Justice. Commission proposed targeted amendments in Jan 2026. ENISA's first State of Cybersecurity in the Union report (Dec 2024) gives a pre-implementation snapshot.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (executive summary SWD(2020) 344), SWD(2020) 345
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (executive summary SWD(2020) 344)
literature.outcomes: incident costs; ICT security spending; authorities' resources
literature.headline: Preferred option may cut the cost of cybersecurity incidents by EUR 11.3bn over ten years; entities in scope would need up to 22% more ICT security spending in the first years (12% for those already covered); authorities' resources up about 20-30%
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected NIS 2 to cut the cost of cyber incidents by EUR 11.3 billion over ten years, while companies newly covered would raise security spending by up to 22%.
literature.quality: forecast; IA notes lack of systematic data

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Evaluation of the functioning of the NIS Directive (Annex 5 of the NIS 2 impact assessment), SWD(2020) 345, Part 2
literature.title: Evaluation of the functioning of the NIS Directive (Annex 5 of the NIS 2 impact assessment)
literature.method: ex-post evaluation (desk research, surveys, country visits)
literature.headline: NIS1 raised awareness and capabilities but scope was too narrow and national identification of operators very inconsistent; no data available to measure NIS1's actual impact on security spending; evaluation limited on effectiveness and efficiency by data gaps
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's review of the first NIS Directive found it changed mindsets but left large gaps between countries - e.g. major hospitals covered in one country but not another - and no data existed to measure its effect on spending.

literature.citation: ENISA (2020), NIS Investments (first edition), ENISA report, 11 Dec 2020
literature.title: NIS Investments (first edition)
literature.method: survey of 251 operators and digital service providers in FR, DE, IT, ES, PL
literature.headline: 82% of respondents said the NIS Directive had a positive effect on their information security; EU organisations spend on average 41% less on information security than US counterparts
literature.summary_plain: In ENISA's first survey, 82% of operators said the first NIS Directive improved their security, though EU firms spent 41% less on security than US firms.

literature.citation: ENISA (2024), NIS Investments 2024, ENISA report, Nov 2024
literature.title: NIS Investments 2024
literature.method: survey of 1,350 organisations, 27 Member States; old-vs-new-sector comparison (descriptive)
literature.headline: Organisations earmark 9.0% of IT investment for information security (+1.9 pp); 89% need more security staff for NIS2; 34% of SMEs cannot request the extra budget; sectors already under NIS1 report higher maturity (e.g. 6.8 vs 6.2 risk management) than newly covered sectors
literature.summary_plain: Pre-NIS 2 baseline: firms spend 9% of IT budgets on security, most expect NIS 2 to raise costs, and sectors already regulated under the first directive report better security than newcomers.
literature.quality: descriptive; old-vs-new sector gap not causal

literature.citation: ENISA (2025), NIS Investments 2025, ENISA report, Dec 2025
literature.title: NIS Investments 2025
literature.outcomes: security spending; compliance drivers; patching; talent
literature.headline: Security spending stable at about 9% of IT budgets (median EUR 1.5m), shifting to technology and outsourcing; compliance is the main investment driver (70%); 28% take over three months to patch critical vulnerabilities; 30% did no assessment in 12 months
literature.summary_plain: In the first year of NIS 2, security budgets held at about 9% of IT spending, compliance drove most investment, but many firms still patch slowly.

literature.title: 2024 Report on the State of Cybersecurity in the Union
literature.headline: First report under NIS2 Art. 18; finds a substantial threat level and broadly aligned national strategies; data collected while transposition ongoing, intended as baseline for later NIS2 assessments
literature.summary_plain: ENISA's first EU-wide state-of-cybersecurity report, intended as the baseline against which NIS 2 will be judged.

literature.summary_plain: Nearly two years after the deadline, four countries had still not fully transposed NIS 2 and were taken to court.

literature.title: ENISA NIS360 - 2024
literature.method: composite maturity/criticality index for 22 NIS2 Annex I (sub)sectors built from an industry survey (93% large firms; same fieldwork as NIS Investments 2024), a survey of national authorities, ENISA incident data (CIRAS) and Eurostat indicators
literature.outcomes: sector cybersecurity maturity and criticality; 'risk zone' sectors
literature.headline: Electricity, telecoms and banking score highest on maturity and criticality, while ICT service management, space, public administrations, maritime, health and gas fall in a 'risk zone' where maturity lags criticality.
literature.summary_plain: ENISA's first sector-by-sector scorecard for the industries covered by NIS2. Long-regulated sectors like power, telecoms and banks are the best prepared; newly covered or weakly supervised sectors such as public administration, health and space are lagging.
literature.quality: Baseline monitoring around the NIS2 transposition deadline; composite index with judgement-based weights, no counterfactual; industry data overlap with NIS Investments 2024
literature.interested_party: ENISA is the EU agency charged with supporting NIS2 implementation
literature.citation: ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) (2025), ENISA NIS360 - 2024, ENISA report (TLP GREEN), February 2025

literature.title: ENISA NIS360 (third edition; press release 'NIS360: The bigger picture on maturity and criticality of NIS critical sectors')
literature.venue: ENISA report and press release, 28 May 2026
literature.method: repeated composite maturity/criticality assessment of NIS2 Annex I sectors (entity surveys, national authority input, EU-level data), compared with the previous edition
literature.outcomes: change in sector cybersecurity maturity; risk-zone membership
literature.headline: Maturity improved across EU critical sectors since the previous edition: trust services, aviation and financial market infrastructures moved into the high-maturity band and gas, road, maritime and health improved within the moderate band, though health, railway, maritime, ICT service management, space, public administrations and water remain in the risk zone.
literature.summary_plain: ENISA's latest scorecard finds critical sectors are getting better at cybersecurity as NIS2 takes hold, with several moving up a band. ENISA links part of the improvement to the new legislation, but progress is uneven and many sectors are still behind.
literature.quality: Before/after comparison of a composite index with no control group; ENISA attributes improvement partly to NIS2 but cannot separate it from threat trends; only press release read
literature.interested_party: ENISA is the EU agency charged with supporting NIS2 implementation
literature.citation: ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) (2026), ENISA NIS360 (third edition; press release 'NIS360: The bigger picture on maturity and criticality of NIS critical sectors'), ENISA report and press release, 28 May 2026

literature.title: Companies Suffered Damage from Cyberattacks and Are Sceptical About NIS-2 (ZEW Information Economy Report Q4 2025)
literature.method: representative business survey of about 1,100 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing (Dec 2025-Jan 2026), about 200 of which expect to be covered by NIS-2
literature.outcomes: self-reported NIS-2 compliance; perceived burden; cyberattack damage
literature.headline: About 57% of firms that consider themselves affected by NIS-2 say they already comply with most rules and 17% do not (fully) comply; around half expect it to strengthen cybersecurity, but about 60% call the administrative burden too high and reporting too extensive.
literature.summary_plain: A large German survey run just after Germany's NIS-2 law came into force. Most affected firms say they mostly comply and half think it will help security, but most also say the paperwork and reporting are too heavy.
literature.quality: Representative survey but only ~200 affected firms; self-reported, one country, right after transposition; press release only
literature.citation: ZEW Mannheim (Daniel Erdsiek, Eliza Stenzhorn) (2026), Companies Suffered Damage from Cyberattacks and Are Sceptical About NIS-2 (ZEW Information Economy Report Q4 2025), ZEW press release / ZEW-Branchenreport Informationswirtschaft

literature.title: NIS Investments 2022
literature.method: survey of 1,080 operators of essential services and digital service providers in all 27 Member States, year-on-year comparison, sector deep dives (energy, health), plus Gartner market data
literature.outcomes: IT and information security budgets; influence of the (first) NIS Directive on investment
literature.headline: Third edition surveying 1,080 OES/DSPs: absolute IT and information-security budgets and the share of IT budgets spent on security were significantly lower than the previous year, partly due to sample composition and COVID-19.
literature.summary_plain: ENISA's yearly survey of companies covered by the original NIS rules, tracking how much they spend on cybersecurity and how the law shapes that spending. It is part of the evidence base behind NIS2.
literature.quality: Predecessor (NIS1) evidence that directly concerns NIS2's scope; self-reported, non-panel sample so year-on-year changes partly reflect composition
literature.interested_party: ENISA is the EU cybersecurity agency
literature.citation: ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) (2022), NIS Investments 2022, ENISA report, 23 November 2022

literature.title: NIS Investments Report 2023
literature.method: survey of 1,080 operators of essential services and digital service providers across the EU27 (fourth edition)
literature.outcomes: cybersecurity budgets and how the NIS Directive influenced investment
literature.headline: Fourth edition presenting data from 1,080 OES/DSPs in all 27 Member States on how they invest their cybersecurity budgets and how the NIS Directive influenced this investment.
literature.summary_plain: The 2023 round of ENISA's survey of companies covered by the NIS rules, intended to show policymakers whether the EU cybersecurity framework is working, just before NIS2 had to be applied.
literature.quality: Predecessor (NIS1) evidence and NIS2 baseline; self-reported survey, no counterfactual; landing page only
literature.interested_party: ENISA is the EU cybersecurity agency
